title: The Spring Cash Gap: Why Gearing Up for Your Busiest Quarter Drains Cash Before It Delivers Any
excerpt: Spring means stock, staff and marketing spend go out the door months before the season's revenue lands. Here is why that gap catches profitable Australian SMEs off guard, and how to fund it on purpose.
content:
Spring begins today across the east coast, and for a lot of owner-led businesses that means the busiest quarter of the year is already underway on the outgoing side of the ledger. Stock is being ordered, casual staff are being rostered, marketing spend is being committed, months before any of it turns into revenue that actually lands in the bank. Nothing here has gone wrong. This is simply what gearing up for a strong season looks like from the inside.

We see the same pattern every year with clients heading into their strongest trading window, whether that is a retailer building stock ahead of the pre-Christmas run, a trades business gearing up for the outdoor season, or a professional services firm lifting capacity for a Q4 push. The business looks busier. On paper, it looks more profitable too. For a few months though, the bank balance tells a different story, and that gap is the part most owners have never actually put a number on.

The Lag Between Spending and Getting Paid

Every dollar spent preparing for a busy quarter, stock, wages, marketing, has to travel a distance before it comes back as cash. Stock sits before it sells. A sale sits as a debtor before it is collected. Trade terms with suppliers rarely match trade terms with customers, so the business is frequently paying its own bills on 14 or 30 day terms while waiting 45 or 60 days to be paid on the other side. That distance is not a flaw in the business. It is the structure of trading, and it gets wider precisely when volume is ramping up, which is exactly when owners are least likely to be watching for it.

The businesses that get caught out are rarely the ones doing badly. They are the ones doing well enough to be busy, without having mapped out which specific week the outgoing cash peaks relative to the incoming cash. When that gap does catch a business by surprise, the usual response is to chase debtors harder or push supplier payments out a little further, both of which work in the short term and both of which put pressure on relationships the business will need again next spring. Cash flow discipline is less about spending less and more about knowing, in advance, exactly where that crossover point sits.

Funded From Whatever Account Happens to Be Open

Ask most owners how they are funding this spring's stock up or staffing lift and the honest answer is usually whatever is available at the time. That might be retained cash reserves, a credit card, or simply letting supplier payments run a little later than usual. None of these choices are wrong in isolation. What makes them expensive is that they were never actually chosen. They were the default that filled the gap once it had already opened, at whatever cost that default happened to carry that week.

A business preparing for its busiest quarter in Brisbane or anywhere else on the east coast has the same options either way, a facility drawn down on purpose, a supplier terms conversation had ahead of time, or a deliberate decision to trade slightly smaller and cash fund the season. The difference between an owner who chooses and an owner who defaults is not the amount of cash required. It is whether the decision was made in September or discovered in November, and whether it was made once, calmly, or three or four times under mounting pressure as the season builds.

What the Forecast Shows You Before the Bank Balance Does

A rolling 13-Week Cash Flow Build run from now through into summer will show, week by week, exactly where the outgoing spend on stock and staff outpaces what is coming in from sales, and by roughly how much. That is the number that turns "we might be tight in a few months" into a specific week, a specific shortfall, and a specific source to cover it. Once the shape of the gap is visible, funding it stops being a scramble and becomes a decision made with the full runway still in front of it.

This is the same forecasting discipline that matters whether the business is in Brisbane, Sydney or Melbourne, and it holds regardless of which industry is driving the seasonal lift. The forecast does not change the fact that spring costs cash before it returns any. It just means the business gets to choose the terms on which it pays that bill, rather than having the terms chosen for it.

None of this needs to wait until the gap is already showing up on a bank statement. If this spring's ramp up feels familiar, a conversation now about what the next thirteen weeks actually look like is worth more than the same conversation in November. Book a discovery call and get the shape of the season mapped before it starts spending your cash for you.

faqs.q: How do I know if my business will hit a cash flow gap this spring?
faqs.a: The clearest way is to build a week by week forecast covering the next thirteen weeks, mapping planned stock, wage and marketing spend against expected collections. A 13-Week Cash Flow Build shows the exact week the gap opens and how wide it gets, rather than leaving the business to find out from the bank balance after the fact.

faqs.q: Why does a profitable quarter sometimes come with a cash flow squeeze?
faqs.a: Profit is recognised when a sale happens, but the cash from that sale often lands weeks or months later, while stock, wages and marketing have to be paid well before then. A genuinely profitable quarter can still be the tightest one on the bank statement, simply because of when the money moves rather than whether it exists.

faqs.q: What is the safest way to fund stock and staff ahead of a busy season?
faqs.a: There is no single right answer, but the safest approach is choosing the funding source deliberately and early, whether that is a facility drawn down on purpose, a supplier terms conversation held ahead of time, or planned use of cash reserves. The costly version is defaulting to whatever is available once the gap has already opened.

faqs.q: How far in advance should a Queensland business plan for its busiest trading quarter?
faqs.a: Most owner-led businesses on the Queensland coast benefit from mapping the season at least thirteen weeks out, since that is roughly the length of time between committing to stock or staffing decisions and seeing the resulting cash land. Planning any later usually means reacting to the gap instead of choosing how to fund it.

faqs.q: Is it normal for debtor days to stretch out during a busy trading period?
faqs.a: Yes. Busier periods often bring more invoices to chase, more customers paying slightly later, and less internal time to follow them up, all of which quietly extends debtor days at exactly the point the business can least afford it. It is a pattern worth watching for rather than a sign that anything has gone wrong.

faqs.q: What does a 13-week cash flow forecast actually show a business owner?
faqs.a: It shows the specific week, the specific shortfall, and the specific cause, whether that is a stock order, a wage lift or a marketing commitment landing before the matching sales are collected. Cash flow discipline comes from seeing that shape early enough to act on it rather than reading about it after the fact.

faqs.q: Should I use a business line of credit to cover a seasonal cash gap?
faqs.a: It can be a sound option if the facility is sized to the actual forecast gap and drawn down on purpose, rather than used as a general buffer. The question worth asking first is not whether credit is available, but exactly how many weeks it needs to cover and what the season's cash flow shows once it is mapped out.
